newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Hurdles remain after Khmer Rouge dissidents' move.
newsitem.headline: Hurdles remain after Khmer Rouge dissidents' move.

text.p: The decision by breakaway Khmer Rouge guerrillas to recognise the authority of the Cambodian government clears a major hurdle to reconciliation but issues remain to be solved, analysts said on Sunday.

Co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen said on Saturday dissident leader Ieng Sary and his supporters in the northwest recognised the authority of the coalition, but this could not immediately be verified by guerrilla representatives.

"They recognise the royal Cambodian government, including the (1994) law that outlawed the Khmer Rouge, and they want their army and people to live with the royal government under one territory, one national administration," said Hun Sen.

He asserted in a public speech that the Khmer Rouge were on their last legs. Their most serious split since the late 1970s emerged in early August when hardliners ordered Ieng Sary's execution after accusing him of embezzlement.
Ieng Sary, former brother-in-law of Khmer Rouge supremo Pol Pot, was foreign minister during the group's 1975-79 "killing fields" rule that left more than one million people dead.
The Khmer Rouge signed a peace accord in 1991 but later reneged on the accord and have been fighting the coalition government that emerged from United Nations-run elections in 1993.

Ranariddh told diplomats on Saturday that Ieng Sary had told negotiators at Thursday's peace talks in Thailand that he was "very happy to see representatives of our royal government" and that he supported a liberal democracy, the monarchy and Buddhism.

Analysts said this was significant as it marked a departure from Ieng Sary's previous insistence that his group and territory were autonomous entities but were ready to discuss reconciliation through his Democratic National United Movement.

Ieng Sary is to clarify his position at a press conference in his Phnom Malai base on Monday, but an analyst said the way was now open for the two sides "to talk about details, about when the government can go in (to guerrilla territory)".
"They are continuing the talks about the nuts and bolts," he said, noting the formation of a joint working committee and adding: "It could take a while."

This was echoed by a senior diplomat, who said news that the guerrillas recognised government authority was significant if confirmed but added it would be wise to "wait and see until the whole thing is secured -- I think there's a long way to go".
The analysts said the fate of Ieng Sary, sentenced to death in absentia for his role in the Khmer Rouge genocide, posed the thorniest problem, although government leaders favour a royal pardon.
An Asian political analyst said both premiers "seem to agree that the Ieng Sary amnesty is important as it will stop the fighting, stop the war and allow for development".
"The military budget...can be cut," the analyst said.

Officials said the guerrillas were particularly anxious to secure an amnesty for their leader, but co-Defence Minister Tea Banh said on Saturday he had told Ieng Sary the government "dare not promise" an amnesty as it was up to King Norodom Sihanouk.

One analyst noted that while Sihanouk has been a vocal advocate of national reconciliation, he also supported a trial for leaders of the 1975-79 Khmer Rouge regime. But observers believe that he will agree to a pardon in the national interest.

The premiers have yet to formally ask the king to grant the amnesty, while parliamentarians are also seeking a debate on how to deal with the dissidents. While major hurdles have been overcome, a concrete agreement could take some time.
